name: Chadian Arabic
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Owens, Jonathan. 1993. A Grammar of Nigerian Arabic (Semitica Viva 10). Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
catalog_locator: Sec. 1.6 'Stress', pp. 42-43, rules (23)-(27); sec. 1.6.1 pp. 43-44 (stress before final-t deletion); sec. 1.6.2 p. 44 (epenthetic vowels); fn. 7 p. 42
catalog_quote: Word stress can be accounted for in the following five rules. (23) Special cases -í "my", aCCáC (comparative), singulative -á, adjectival formative – íy(y) The first person possessive pronoun, comparative adjectives and singulative -á in certain stems (see 2.13) are stressed on the final syllable. ... Also, loan words often keep their original stress (sometimes even tone) patterns ... (24) First VCC/VVC heavy syllable) from end is stressed, provided it is not more than 3 syllables from end. náadata "she called him", náadat "she called", náada "he called", tináad "you m call", marḍáan "sick", ... támmat "it f finished", bitímm "it finishes" ... (25a) Antepenult CV́CVCV(C) If there are three successive short syllables (no more no less), stress falls on the antepenultimate. ḍáraba "he hit him", ḍárabak "he hit you", ... fíhimat "she understood" (25b) If the second syllable from the end contains an epenthetic vowel (introduced by 1.4.1, underlined here), and no heavy syllables occur, the antepenultimate is stressed ... (26) Penultimate In all other cases it is on the penultimate (or on the only syllable of monosyllabic words). ḍárab "he hit", ʼíḍiš "he was thirsty", kábiš "ram", ráaṣ "head", fóog "on". In words of four or more syllables, with the last three syllables open, the penultimate is stressed, with secondary stress (grave accent) on the fourth from end. ... It should be noted that in the Eastern dialect, disyllabic CVCV(C) stems are stressed on the last syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: chad1249 (Chadian Arabic) is not in the catalog. All 11 works with stress in the title are false attachments: none concerns Chadian Arabic (they are general phase-theory/phrasal-stress papers, English radio-news phonetics, Japanese pitch accent, Ojibwa stress, Jamaican English accent attitudes, and motor-control rhythm papers); the shared title words 'phase' and 'radio' suggest an automatic Glottolog language assignment, so none was downloaded and all get priority 'none'. The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Owens 1993, A Grammar of Nigerian Arabic, sec. 1.6 pp. Chad-proper sources held by the project (Jullien de Pommerol 1999 pp. 20-21) give only long-vowel high pitch, no stress rule; Abu Absi & Sinaud 1966/1968 (four volumes, two newly downloaded from archive. Manfredi & Roset 2021 and Kaye & Rosenhouse 1997 are second-hand and agree with Owens. Highest-priority unobtained item: Roth-Laly 1994b 'Le cas de l'accent dans l'aire tchado-sudanaise' (Publications Langues'O), then Zeltner & Tourneux 1986 p. 72 and Kaye 1976;org, Google Books API, Gallica SRU and HathiTrust catalog probes were run (Gallica/HathiTrust could not be reached by automated download; no open copies of Roth-Laly 1994b, Lethem 1920 or Carbou 1913 located). new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the saved page scan, and publisher-authorised Google Books preview of Owens 1993, A Grammar of Nigerian Arabic, Harrassowitz) and read them directly (not via scanned). p. 42, sec. 1.6 Stress: 'Word stress can be accounted for in the following five rules. (23) Special cases -í "my", aCCáC (comparative)7, singulative -á, adjectival formative – íy(y).. are stressed on the final syllable'.. 'Also, loan words often keep their original stress (sometimes even tone) patterns'.. '(24) First VCC/VVC heavy syllable) from end is stressed, provided it is not more than 3 syllables from end.' (náadata, náadat, tináad, mardáan, bahaayímna).. '(25a) Antepenult CV́CVCV(C) If there are three successive…
new_statements.rule_in_words: weight-sensitive with a three-syllable window: certain suffixes/patterns (-í 'my', comparative aCCáC, singulative -á, -íy(y)-e) and unassimilated loans carry lexical/final stress; otherwise stress the rightmost heavy (long-vowel+C or VCC) syllable if it is among the last three; if the last three syllables are all light (exactly three, or with an epenthetic penult) stress the antepenult; otherwise the penult (náada, dárab, kábiš). Prefixes an-, al-, am- are outside the stress domain. Eastern (Bagirmi) dialect: disyllabic CVCV(C) stems take final stress (katáb, bagár vs Western kátab, bágar). Stress is assigned before final-t deletion, yielding the minimal pair kátab 'he wrote' vs katáb 'I wrote'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 43: 'In words of four or more syllables, with the last three syllables open, the penultimate is stressed, with secondary stress (grave accent) on the fourth from end' (dàrabáta 'she hit him', gàabaláta 'she met him').
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on -í 'my', comparatives aCCáC, singulative -á, adjectival -íy(y) before f.sg -e; loanwords often keep source stress or tone (gadé, gangá < Kanuri; háwsá < Hausa); epenthetic vowels (except the 25b case) are stressable (bagúnṣa); an-/al-/am- prefixes never stressed; Eastern dialect final stress on CVCV(C) stems and on epenthetic vowel in timíš 'you m go'; footnote 7: in E the comparative is stressed on the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules stated over citation/inflected word forms of the Western (Kirenawa/Maiduguri) dialect; author marks primary stress with acute and secondary with grave; definite article and other proclitic prefixes excluded from the stress word. Jullien de Pommerol 1999:20 (N'Djamena Chadian Arabic, saved) independently characterises the prominence as pitch-like ('accentuation.. proche d'une variation tonale') carried by long vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Owens 1993 describes Nigerian (Shuwa/Borno) Arabic, basically the Western dialect of Kirenawa/Maiduguri (Glottolog lists Owens 1993 under chad1249; WALS 'Arabic (Borno Nigerian)' also maps to chad1249). Owens notes a dialect split inside the language: Western kátab vs Eastern ('Bagirmi Arabic', E Nigeria into Chad) katáb, i.e. Eastern disyllabic CVCV(C) stems are stressed finally. Jullien de Pommerol 1999 describes the N'Djamena-based vehicular Chadian Arabic and speaks of a pitch-like 'accentuation' on long vowels rather than giving a syllable-position rule. Roth 1979 (Abbéché, eastern Chad) and Zeltner & Tourneux 1986 (Ulâd Eli) describe other chad1249 varieties and were not accessible.

new_statements.citation: Owens, Jonathan (1993). A Grammar of Nigerian Arabic (Semitica Viva 10). Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz. Sec. 1.6 'Stress', pp. 42-44.
new_statements.reading: First-hand, explicit weight-sensitive system for Western Nigerian (Shuwa) Arabic, which Glottolog files under chad1249: stress the rightmost heavy (VVC/VCC) syllable within a three-syllable right-edge window; with no heavy syllable, antepenult when the word is exactly three light syllables (dáraba) or when the penult vowel is epenthetic; otherwise penult (dárab, kábiš), monosyllables stressed; prefixes an-/al-/am- are extrametrical; lexical exceptions with final stress (-í 'my', comparatives, singulative -á, loans). The Eastern Nigerian dialect (and per Manfredi & Roset 2021 / Kaye & Rosenhouse 1997, Chadian Baggara varieties) stresses disyllabic CVCV(C) stems finally, giving a contrast kátab 'he wrote' vs katáb 'I wrote'. Caveat: Owens describes Nigeria, not Chad proper; Chad-side first-hand statements (Roth-Laly 1994b, Zeltner & Tourneux 1986) were not obtained.

sources.quote: Il semble que l'arabe parlé au Tchad utilise une accentuation caractéristique proche d'une variation tonale. Les voyelles longues sont prononcées légèrement au-dessus de la tonalité ordinaire. Chaque mot de plusieurs syllabes ayant généralement une voyelle longue acquiert ainsi une modulation particulière.

sources.citation: Kaye, Alan S. & Judith Rosenhouse. 1997. Arabic dialects and Maltese. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 263-311. London: Routledge. pp. 280-281 'Stress'.
sources.quote: The Chadian-Nigerian area is complicated as there is a major dichotomy between kátab 'he wrote' (Gawalme) vs. katáb (Balge). The same situation occurs in CVCVCV words. The original PCA stress on the first syllable, has been preserved in Ca. sámaka 'fish', Sudan bágara 'cow', Chad. séjera 'tree', Bag. and Jugari hájara 'stone'
sources.note: Second-hand survey remarks: 'The Chadian-Nigerian area is complicated as there is a major dichotomy between kátab (Gawalme) vs. katáb (Balge)'; original first-syllable stress in CVCVCV preserved in 'Chad. šéjera tree'; Nigerian Arabic stresses 1sg -í (usubí 'my finger') and álmi/aláxu-type initial CVC.
